part_title: CloudFront Edge Delivery, Secure Origins and Cache Policies

scenes.title: CloudFront CDN Request Flow
scenes.narration: Follow the user request into the CloudFront edge location, and then distinguish the two arrows: a cache hit returns an existing object straight from the edge, while a cache miss goes to the origin, shown as an S3 bucket, stores the returned content at the edge and serves it to the user. The example headers below show X-Cache Hit from cloudfront and Miss from cloudfront. The Age header illustrates how long a cached response has been at the edge; neither header proves that every viewer sees the same cached entry. In the console walkthrough, create a distribution, select the origin, wait for deployment, and make repeated requests. A first request can already be a hit if another request populated that cache. The performance benefit is reduced origin load and lower latency for reusable objects. Never assume an individualized generative AI response is automatically safe to cache.

scenes.title: CloudFront origins:
scenes.narration: Compare the three columns. A private S3 origin uses Origin Access Control so the bucket stays private and the distribution is authorized to retrieve objects. The center illustrates a VPC origin, such as an Application Load Balancer in a VPC, where CloudFront can access supported private resources using the appropriate configuration. The third uses a public HTTP or HTTPS endpoint, such as a separately hosted server. These are distinct trust and networking models. In the console examples, notice that the origin type, domain, access control, and protocol policy change between columns. An S3 website endpoint is a custom origin rather than the private S3 bucket origin protected by OAC, which is a common source of confusion. Do not simply expose a backend to the public internet for convenience. Choose the origin configuration after considering authentication, the backend exposure boundary, encryption, caching, and operational permissions.

scenes.title: S3 OAC and Bucket Policy: Block Public Access, Authorized Distribution Only
scenes.narration: This diagram has two routes to the same private S3 bucket. Requests through the CloudFront distribution can succeed when the Origin Access Control signs the origin request and the bucket policy authorizes that particular distribution. A direct public S3 object URL is blocked. Follow the setup sequence beneath the diagram: create an OAC, associate it with the S3 origin, update the S3 bucket policy, and test both paths. The policy illustration uses the CloudFront service principal, s3 GetObject on bucket objects, and a SourceArn condition limited to the distribution ARN. Substitute your real distribution and bucket identifiers rather than copying example strings. Keep S3 Block Public Access enabled as intended. The sample output contrasts an HTTP two hundred response through CloudFront with an HTTP four hundred three from direct S3 access. Remember that this secures access to the origin, not necessarily viewer access at the edge; separately consider signed URLs or other viewer-side authorization if needed.

scenes.title: Cache policies: TTL and cache keys
scenes.narration: The upper half contrasts a reusable static asset with a personalized AI chat answer. TTL settings determine how long CloudFront can retain an eligible response; the minimum, default, and maximum values constrain cache behavior in conjunction with applicable origin headers. The cache key determines which requests are considered equivalent, using only the headers, cookies, and query-string values selected in the policy. Adding unnecessary values to the key reduces cache reuse. Excluding a value that actually changes the response can leak or serve incorrect data. The lab proposes one behavior for static assets like JavaScript and images, and a second behavior for an AI route with caching disabled. Trace the static request to an edge hit and the personalized request to its origin. Be especially careful with authenticated requests, user identifiers, and generated responses. Review cache and origin request policies together; forwarding a field to the origin does not necessarily make it part of the cache key.

scenes.title: CloudFront vs. S3 Cross-Region Replication
scenes.narration: The two diagrams solve different problems. On the left, CloudFront places reusable content in edge caches close to users. When that content is absent or expired, CloudFront fetches it from the configured origin. This optimizes reads and reduces origin traffic, but it is not an independent region-to-region backup strategy. On the right, S3 Cross-Region Replication asynchronously copies eligible objects between buckets in different AWS Regions. The example takes a source bucket in us east one and a destination in eu west one, sets a replication rule and IAM permissions, then verifies the object appears after a delay. Replicated objects are actual destination objects and may be read or written according to bucket policy; replicas are not inherently read-only. Replication lag, versioning prerequisites, rule filters, and delete marker behavior should be evaluated for the design. Cache expiry and invalidation are different from replication completion. For a global AI frontend, CloudFront may accelerate static assets while replication serves separate durability, regional access, or recovery requirements.
